title: Diwali Sweets Cost More This Year as Sugar and Ghee Prices Climb Together
excerpt: Sugar is up 29.8% year on year and ghee 10-15%, so the same box of kaju katli takes a bigger share of the festive budget — and shops are split between raising prices and absorbing the hit.
body:
• Diwali sweets cost more this year because the ingredients moved together: official data show sugar prices up 29.8% year on year in September and inflation in the sugar, confectionery and dessert category at 13.8%.
  • Sweet makers report ghee and butter costs up 10-15% and milk-driven costs up as much as 25-30% for khoya-heavy sweets; retail sweet prices are rising roughly 10-15% this festive season.
  • Shops are splitting on strategy: some pass costs on, others absorb most of the increase and shrink box sizes instead.
  • What this means for your budget: a kilo of kaju katli or a premium gift box will take a visibly bigger share of the Diwali budget this year — in Telangana, families report the sweet bill leaving a bigger hole than last Diwali, so price the mithai run before the gift list, not after.

The Diwali sweet box is where festive inflation shows up first, and this year it is showing up in Hyderabad and across Telangana, where families say sweet prices are leaving a bigger hole in their Diwali budgets. The reason is not one expensive ingredient but all of them at once: sugar, milk, ghee and dry fruits have climbed together into the peak season, according to Indulge Express's analysis of official price data.

The numbers behind the mithai bill

Inflation in the sugar, confectionery and dessert category climbed to 13.8 per cent in September, with standalone sugar prices jumping 29.8 per cent year on year. Non-milk prepared sweets rose 9.4 per cent and candy 11.5 per cent. Sugar's rise is structural: lower production and the diversion of nearly 30 lakh tonnes of cane to ethanol tightened supply, pushing the all-India average retail price to ₹64.24 a kilogram by August 30, while jaggery — the fallback sweetener — roughly doubled in some markets to ₹80-90 a kilogram, according to Local Samosa's market reporting. Dry fruits compounded it: raisin and munakka inflation touched 10.4 per cent in September and cashews rose 4 per cent, hitting kaju katli and dry-fruit laddoos hardest.

How sweet shops are responding

Makers describe a squeeze they cannot fully pass on. Vadodara's Jagdish Farshan, an 88-year-old sweets house, says butter and ghee procurement costs are up about 10 to 15 per cent from last Diwali, and plans roughly a 10 per cent retail increase while absorbing about 10 per cent of the cost jump itself. Kolkata-origin Sweet Bengal reports input costs up 25 to 30 per cent, mostly from milk, but plans only a 1 to 2 per cent price rise and will absorb the rest; Bengaluru's Lal Sweets, facing butter, ghee and sugar costs up 12 to 15 per cent, is holding prices for now. Listed snacks maker Bikaji has already raised prices twice in recent months and says it will hold through Diwali. Smaller shops feel it fastest: Jaipur's Tyohaar Sweets says the cost of making mawa-based mithai rose from roughly $2.60-$3.10 a kilogram to about $4.15, with only limited 5 per cent retail hikes so far.

How families are adjusting

The pattern at the counter is smaller, more deliberate buying: curated sampler boxes instead of full assortments, handmade sweets at home where the math still works, and gift budgets shifted toward smaller boxes bought earlier. Relief, when it comes, hinges on the new sugarcane crushing cycle stabilising wholesale rates. Until then, the Diwali sweet run costs more for the same box — and in Telangana's sweet shops, that difference is the conversation at every counter.
